title: Traffic replay: quant routing behavior on mixed cold/warm workloads
content:
Summary:
This doc captures an experiment run that replays a production-like traffic mix through the serving runtime to observe how quantization choices (INT8, AWQ, GPTQ, FP8) and kernel selection interact with cold vs warm state. We focused on per-request latency tail behavior, token cost, and a lightweight quality check (log-prob drift + sample-based pass/fail on a small eval set). Goal is to surface concrete failure modes and quick mitigation paths for canary routing rules.

Key motivation / questions:
- We have anecdotal reports of tail spikes when switching kernels mid-request under mixed workloads; is this correlated with quant routing fallbacks?
- How quickly does KV-prefix caching amortize the extra compute from higher-precision fallbacks?
- For a realistic customer mix (short chat + few long doc syntheses + embeddings bursts), which quant config gives the best latency/quality/cost envelope without needing per-request manual overrides?

Hypothesis:
1) INT8/GPTQ maintain good p50 but suffer p95 when kernel switchover happens or when cache miss rate is high.
2) AWQ degrades quality on a small fraction of prompts (notably code snippets) and sometimes triggers model variant fallback in routing, causing latency spikes.
3) FP8 has predictable latencies and fewer fallbacks but higher token cost.

Environment:
- Cluster: dedicated dev pool (a-size2-gpu-rt) with A100 80GB nodes, kernel builds: linux-x86-rt-2026-07-branch (custom scheduler).
- Serving binary: v0.42.1-quant-experiments.
- Models: rwi/gpt-large-anyon (fp16 baseline), rwi/gpt-large-int8-gptq, rwi/gpt-large-awq, rwi/gpt-large-fp8-opt (FP8 experimental).
- Client replay harness: replay-tokens-v2 (randomized user-session interleaving, preserves original per-session ordering).
- Workload mix: 65% short chat (1–3 turns, 20–60 tokens), 25% medium assistants (100–400 tokens), 10% long synth (500–2000 tokens). Embeddings bursts every 6 minutes (short-lived).
- Cache settings: KV cache enabled for all runs. Measured both cold-start (empty cache) and warm (prewarmed with 24h session prefix distribution).
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency per request, token/sec, GPU util, kernel switch events, fallback events (routing->higher-precision), quality delta: average log-prob drift vs fp16 baseline, sample fail-rate on 120 prompt eval set (semantic + code + math).

What we ran (matrix):
- Config A: INT8 (GPTQ), default kernel selector. Cold and warm.
- Config B: AWQ (AWQ-specific kernel), default selector. Cold and warm.
- Config C: FP8 (experimental runtime path), default selector. Cold and warm.
- Config D: fp16 baseline. Cold and warm (control).
- Each run: 4h steady replay, repeated twice on different nodes to account for placement variance.

High-level results (observations):
- p50: All quant configs close to baseline within 5–8% for short chat. FP8 ~ +2% vs fp16. INT8/GPTQ ~ -10% cost but similar p50.
- p95/p99 tails: INT8/GPTQ showed median p95 ~+40ms compared to baseline in warm runs, but in cold runs spikes were worse (+120–250ms) correlated with kernel switch events logged when a long synthesis request arrived and cache miss rate was high.
- AWQ: had intermittent quality failures on code/math prompts (fail-rate ~5% on our eval set) and when those failures occurred routing layer triggered fallback to fp16 variant for affected requests -> large latency penalty (+350–700ms) for those requests due to model variant switch and cold kernel init.
- FP8: most stable tail (p95 within +15ms of fp16), but overall token GPU seconds cost ~+22% vs INT8; fewer fallback events.
- KV cache effect: warm runs dramatically reduced tail spikes for INT8; amortization point observed after ~10k token prefixes (approx 30s of sustained session activity). Cold-run spikes were primarily due to repeated cache misses on long-context requests where prefix > 1024 tokens; once KV filled, latency normalized.

Detailed notes / traces:
- Kernel switch trace: saw series of kernel handshake logs at time of long-synthesis start (t0). The runtime scheduled an alternate kernel (fallback to safer fp32-ish kernel) after per-layer flakiness counters exceeded threshold. Those counters incremented on unexpected nan/inf or on relative accuracy drop exceeding 0.12 on internal quick-check.
- Fallback triggering pattern: low-precision kernels sometimes produce activation ranges outside expected windows when attention sparsity increases (observed on doc summarization prompts with many rare tokens). This triggered per-layer safety trip which then escalated at routing layer to pick a compatible model variant.
- Embeddings bursts: embedding requests are handled by a different endpoint; we saw queueing interplay where large embedding bursts (short but heavy) temporarily saturated GPU SM and increased decoder latency of ongoing generation by 7–14%. Quant modes didn't change this pattern much.

Quality results (quick eval):
- Log-prob drift avg (vs fp16): INT8: -0.8 nats/token (some variance), AWQ: -1.6 nats/token (peak on code prompts), FP8: -0.15 nats/token.
- Eval pass-rate (120 prompts): fp16: 0 failures, FP8: 1 failure (fuzzy match), INT8: 3 failures (two were borderline semantics), AWQ: 6 failures (4 code-related).

Actionable takeaways:
1) For mixed customer traffic, pure INT8 routing is cost-effective but requires smarter cold-start mitigation. Suggest warmup policy for long-context routes (prepopulate KV for known session prefixes or run small warmup stub).
2) AWQ currently has non-trivial quality regressions on code and math — not ready as default routing for developer-heavy customers. Consider AWQ only for short-chat lightweight routes where quality risk is acceptable.
3) FP8 looks promising as a default safe low-tail option when cost budget permits. It reduced fallbacks and tail jitter, predictable dev experience.
4) Change detection thresholds: our per-layer safety counters are too aggressive for certain attention patterns; tune thresholds to account for attention sparsity distributions in production.
5) Kernel init cost: caching warm kernels per-node and faster lazy init reduces fallback latency by ~60% in our micro runs. Prioritize kernel caching improvements for canary nodes.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How often do real customers hit the long-synthesis path and what is acceptable p99? Need PM/CS to provide two canonical tenant traces.
- Can we add a background, low-cost comparator (cheap token-level check) to catch quality regressions earlier before escalating to model variant fallback?
- Is there a hybrid routing policy that prefers AWQ for short (<60 token) interactions and routes medium/long to FP8? Need A/B plan.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [Priya] File a perf ticket to add warm-kernel cache LRU in scheduler (RD-3216).
- [Ethan] Run a follow-up replay focusing only on code-heavy sessions with higher sampling to validate AWQ regressions.
- [Miguel] Prototype hybrid routing policy in canary: AWQ for short-chat, FP8 for long-synthesis.
- Add more representative customer traces (ask CS for 2 anonymized session logs).

Appendix (quick runbook snippets):
- How to reproduce: run replay harness with --preserve-session-order --kv-prewarm=0/1 to toggle cold/warm; config flags: --quant-config=(int8|awq|fp8|fp16) --kernel-selector=default.
- Logs to inspect: kernel-handshake.log, fallback-events.log, routing-decisions.log. Grab pprof dumps at 5s interval during a spike.

Notes to self:
- This doc is a working capture; still need to sanity-check sample seeds used in eval (randomized).
- Consider adding a small synthetic prompt set that intentionally triggers attention sparsity to reproduce per-layer trips deterministically.
